paras: The lynching of Clark and Bardeau was the hanging of two accused robbers, known as Clark, alias "Butch", and "Frenchy" Bardeau, from a cottonwood tree in Socorro, New Mexico Territory, on the night of 6 October 1881. Arrested on suspicion of robbing a store at Lamy, the two were taken from guard by a "committee" and left hanging under a placard reading "The fate of footpads and horse thieves." The story ran in papers across the country, and within weeks territorial papers cited it in complaints about mob rule at Socorro.

About ten days before the hanging, four men entered the Browne & Manzanares store at Lamy, made everyone present hold up their hands, robbed it in daylight, and rode off on horses belonging to the firm. According to the Chicago Tribune's Socorro correspondent, three heavily armed men later rode into Socorro and were watched but left alone until one of their horses was identified as stolen from Lamy. Officers then arrested two of them after a chase, while the third escaped.

The Tribune reported that the prisoners' boots were full of stolen revolvers and knives, and that they "openly confessed the robbery" and boasted of it. They were heavily chained and put under guard, and a committee "quietly agreed" that "desperate means had to be taken with desperate men."

On Thursday night the two were hanged together from a cottonwood on Methodist avenue, near a spot the Tribune called Death Alley, "chained arm to arm and foot to foot." Residents found the bodies early Friday morning, 7 October, and they were left hanging for several hours with the placard pinned to their backs. The Tribune named the men as "Bushy" Clark, said to be an old offender from "the Allison and Stockton horsethieves of Durango," and "Frenchy" Bardeau, of whom little was known. The Denver Republican's wire gave the names as Clark, alias "Butch", and "Frenchy", formerly of "the notorious Stockton gang"; no account gives their race.

No report of an inquest or of any arrest of the lynchers appears in the coverage. Two weeks later the Las Vegas Gazette noted a fresh street robbery at Socorro and wrote that the Methodist avenue cottonwoods "will have to be called into service again." In early November the "Socorro mob" drove the prosecuting attorney, Frank Chavez, out of town after an acquittal in a separate murder case, and the Gazette wrote that such "hanging scrapes" were doing the town lasting damage. The Arizona Weekly Enterprise, reporting the district attorney's expulsion, added that the two men the mob had hanged for stealing had since been found innocent.

New Mexico and Western papers carried the news first and in a light tone. The Las Vegas Gazette headlined the "Tight Rope Entertainment" and wrote that the placard showed "Socorro is a bad place for bad men," while the Cheyenne Daily Leader titled the Denver wire "Exit 'Butch' and 'Frenchy.'" The Chicago Tribune printed the longest account under "A Neck-Tie Sociable," pairing the committee's reasoning with a description of residents "surprised and horrified" and of the men's "horrible death from strangulation."

Elsewhere the story traveled as a one- or two-sentence wire item, from the Sacramento Daily Record-Union and the Memphis Daily Appeal to weeklies in Ohio, Iowa, Missouri, Minnesota and Alabama. Many digests folded it together with the separate lynching of William Nicholson at Saunders Station, so that the New-York Tribune and the Richmond Dispatch reported "three men" or "Two Robbers and a Murderer" lynched in New Mexico.

The Connecticut Western News reported that lynchers who had hanged one robber at Socorro then hanged two of their own number found on stolen horses; the Socorro specials and the wires describe only two victims, arrested on Wednesday by the Gazette's account and Thursday by the Tribune's. The men's guilt is also disputed: the Chicago Tribune said they confessed, while the Arizona Weekly Enterprise said the two men hanged by the Socorro mob were later found innocent, without naming them. Only the Sacramento copy of the Denver wire placed the robbery at "Laramie"; the local specials and other copies give Lamy.

bases: Two men arrested by officers and held under guard were taken out at night by a 'committee' and hanged from a cottonwood in Socorro (A6, A2, A9).

Two prisoners accused of robbery and horse theft were hanged without trial by a 'Vigilance Committee' or 'mob' (A9, A37, A6), whose placard called it 'The fate of footpads and horse thieves' (A2, A6); the size of the group is not given, but a committee and mob imply more than three.

Separate specials from Socorro to the Las Vegas Gazette and the Chicago Tribune, a Denver Republican special and a Santa Fe dispatch agree on the double hanging at Socorro (A2, A6, A1, A9); only the victims' guilt is disputed (A41).

framing.detail: The Las Vegas Gazette headlined the 'Tight Rope Entertainment' and wrote that the placard 'shows that Socorro is a bad place for bad men.'
The Chicago Tribune called it 'A Neck-Tie Sociable', repeated the committee's reasoning about 'desperate men', and also described residents as 'horrified' and the deaths as 'horrible'.
Most papers ran the Denver wire in a sentence or two, often folded with the Nicholson lynching into 'three men lynched'.
Later Gazette items joked that the Methodist avenue cottonwoods 'will have to be called into service again' but also said the 'hanging scrapes' were damaging Socorro.
The Arizona Weekly Enterprise said the hanged men were found innocent and that Socorro was 'given over to violence and mob law.'
